comments.author: helmholtzhum
comments.text: The acoustics explanation is mostly right but conflates two mechanisms. The cover-as-bell ringing (impact excitation from tires) and the cavity resonance (the shaft acting as a Helmholtz resonator when rain changes the effective neck geometry) are different phenomena with different pitches. The article's spectrogram actually shows both — two distinct bands — and labels them as one.

replies.author: stormdrain
replies.text: OP here — fair hit. I noticed the two bands and mentioned it in a footnote but should have promoted it to the main text. A follow-up with a proper two-mechanism model is in the works; a civil engineer reader has offered access to a test shaft, which is the most niche perk I've ever been offered.

replies.author: helmholtzhum
replies.text: Looking forward to it. Measure with the cover seated and unseated if you can — the bell mode should shift, the cavity mode shouldn't.

comments.author: pagetable
comments.text: Anecdote: there was a cover on my old commute that sang a clean minor third above the road noise in the rain, dead reliable. Then a utility crew replaced it and the new one was silent. I was unreasonably sad about it. Streets have voices; maintenance changes the choir.

comments.author: tokenring
comments.text: Municipal trivia: some cities spec covers with anti-rock inserts specifically to kill the ringing, because residents log it as noise complaints. The singing described here is, from the city's perspective, a defect. One person's found sound is another person's ticket queue.
